concepts.label: Multiple sclerosis classically presents with relapsing attacks of motor and sensory paraesthesia, correlating with demyelinating plaques on imaging
concepts.article_title: The relapsing clinical presentation of multiple sclerosis
concepts.definition: Multiple sclerosis is a chronic autoimmune, demyelinating disease of the central nervous system. Its classic clinical course (relapsing-remitting MS, the commonest subtype) is one of discrete attacks of neurological dysfunction — commonly motor weakness and sensory disturbance/paraesthesia, but potentially involving any CNS pathway (optic neuritis, cerebellar signs, bladder dysfunction) — followed by partial or complete recovery. These attacks correlate anatomically with demyelinating plaques that are disseminated in time and space, visualised on MRI as characteristic periventricular and other white-matter lesions, which underpins the clinical/radiological diagnostic criteria for the disease.
concepts.explicit_objective: State that multiple sclerosis classically presents with relapsing attacks of motor and sensory paraesthesia, correlating with demyelinating plaques on imaging.
concepts.pitfalls: Confusing MS's relapsing clinical/radiological presentation (the diagnostic picture) with its acute-attack treatment (high-dose IV methylprednisolone) or its disease-modifying treatment when first-line therapy fails (natalizumab) — presentation, acute treatment and maintenance treatment are three distinct, separately testable facts about the same disease.
concepts.original_wording: Source item 11 ("multiple sclerosis / Attacks of motor sensory paresthesia, CT plaques and demylenation"), embedded-answer format, read from EOM - paper 2 cns 2019.pdf, p2.
concepts.asu_field_note: Tested as item 11 of EOM - paper 2 cns 2019.pdf (src_c0416316a05f729b9aaf), p2.

concepts.label: Medulloblastoma is a childhood embryonal tumour of the posterior cranial fossa, classically midline, composed of sheets of primitive cells
concepts.article_title: Medulloblastoma as a paediatric posterior fossa embryonal tumour
concepts.definition: Medulloblastoma is the most common malignant paediatric brain tumour, classically arising in the cerebellum/roof of the fourth ventricle within the posterior cranial fossa, typically midline (in the cerebellar vermis) in young children (a peak around 5 years old). Histologically it is a highly cellular embryonal tumour composed of sheets of small, primitive (poorly differentiated) round blue cells, reflecting its origin from primitive neuroectodermal precursor cells; it can obstruct the fourth ventricle, causing hydrocephalus, and has a propensity to spread via the CSF ("drop metastases").
concepts.explicit_objective: State that medulloblastoma is a childhood embryonal tumour of the posterior cranial fossa, classically midline, composed of sheets of primitive cells.
concepts.pitfalls: Confusing medulloblastoma (childhood, midline posterior fossa, sheets of primitive cells) with oligodendroglioma (adult, cerebral hemispheres, characteristic "fried-egg" clear-halo cells) — both are CNS tumours but with distinct age groups, locations and histology.
concepts.original_wording: Source item 13 ("medullablastoma / Child 5 yrs in posterior cranial fossa midline, Sheets of primitive cells (embryonal tumor)"), embedded-answer format, read from EOM - paper 2 cns 2019.pdf, p2.
concepts.asu_field_note: Tested as item 13 of EOM - paper 2 cns 2019.pdf (src_c0416316a05f729b9aaf), p2.

concepts.label: The fourth pharyngeal pouch gives rise to the superior parathyroid glands
concepts.article_title: The fourth pharyngeal pouch and the superior parathyroid glands
concepts.definition: The pharyngeal (branchial) pouches are paired embryonic endodermal outpocketings that give rise to distinct adult structures. The fourth pharyngeal pouch gives rise to the superior parathyroid glands (along with the ultimobranchial body, which contributes calcitonin-secreting C cells to the thyroid). This is distinct from the third pharyngeal pouch, which gives rise to the inferior parathyroid glands and the thymus — the third pouch's parathyroid derivative migrates further caudally during development than the fourth's, which is why the "inferior" parathyroids (from the third pouch) can end up more variable in final position than the "superior" ones (from the fourth pouch).
concepts.explicit_objective: State that the fourth pharyngeal pouch gives rise to the superior parathyroid glands.
concepts.pitfalls: Confusing the fourth pharyngeal pouch's derivative (superior parathyroid glands) with the third pharyngeal pouch's derivatives (inferior parathyroid glands and the thymus) — a classic source of embryology exam confusion given the counter-intuitive numbering (third pouch to inferior gland, fourth pouch to superior gland).
concepts.original_wording: Source item 15 ("superior parathyroid / Fourth pharyngeal pouch gives (embryology)"), embedded-answer format, read from EOM - paper 2 cns 2019.pdf, p2.
concepts.asu_field_note: Tested as item 15 of EOM - paper 2 cns 2019.pdf (src_c0416316a05f729b9aaf), p2.

concepts.label: The lateral geniculate body of the thalamus receives its input from the optic tract
concepts.article_title: The optic tract as the input to the lateral geniculate body
concepts.definition: The visual pathway runs from the retina via the optic nerve to the optic chiasm (where nasal retinal fibres decussate), continuing as the optic tract, which carries visual information from the contralateral visual field of both eyes. The optic tract terminates in, and provides the principal input to, the lateral geniculate body (nucleus) of the thalamus, the main subcortical relay station for conscious vision; from there, geniculocalcarine (optic radiation) fibres project to the primary visual cortex in the occipital lobe.
concepts.explicit_objective: State that the lateral geniculate body of the thalamus receives its input from the optic tract.
concepts.pitfalls: Confusing the optic tract (post-chiasmal, carries the contralateral visual field, terminates in the lateral geniculate body) with the optic nerve (pre-chiasmal, carries one eye's entire visual field) — a lesion of each produces a different visual field deficit.
concepts.original_wording: Source item 19 ("optic tract / LGB receives inputs from"), embedded-answer format, read from EOM - paper 2 cns 2019.pdf, p2.
concepts.asu_field_note: Tested as item 19 of EOM - paper 2 cns 2019.pdf (src_c0416316a05f729b9aaf), p2.

concepts.label: The great cerebral vein (of Galen) is found within the cistern of the ambient (cisterna ambiens)
concepts.article_title: The great cerebral vein's location in the cisterna ambiens
concepts.definition: The great cerebral vein (of Galen) is a short, midline venous structure formed by the union of the two internal cerebral veins, which then curves posteriorly around the splenium of the corpus callosum before draining into the straight sinus. Along this posterior course, it lies within the cisterna ambiens (the ambient/quadrigeminal cistern region), a CSF-filled subarachnoid space that wraps around the midbrain; this cisternal location is a distinct anatomical fact from the vein's formation (union of the two internal cerebral veins) and matters clinically because it is a recognised site for vein-of-Galen malformations to present within this cistern.
concepts.explicit_objective: State that the great cerebral vein (of Galen) is found within the cisterna ambiens.
concepts.subtopic: Venous drainage of the head and neck
concepts.module_subject: ASU-CNS-3 > Anatomy > Venous drainage of the head and neck
concepts.pitfalls: Confusing the great cerebral vein's location (within the cisterna ambiens, around the midbrain) with its formation (union of the two internal cerebral veins) — both are true, testable facts about the same vein but answer different questions.
concepts.original_wording: Source item 21 ("great cerebral vein / Found in cisterna ambiens"), embedded-answer format, read from EOM - paper 2 cns 2019.pdf, p3.
concepts.asu_field_note: Tested as item 21 of EOM - paper 2 cns 2019.pdf (src_c0416316a05f729b9aaf), p3.

concepts.label: Forceps major is a commissural fibre of the corpus callosum connecting the two occipital lobes
concepts.article_title: Forceps major as a commissural fibre of the corpus callosum
concepts.definition: White matter fibres of the cerebrum are classified as association (connecting areas within the same hemisphere), projection (connecting the cortex to lower centres) or commissural (connecting the two hemispheres). Forceps major (the occipital/posterior forceps) is formed by fibres of the splenium of the corpus callosum sweeping posteriorly into each occipital lobe, connecting the two occipital lobes across the midline — it is therefore classified as a commissural fibre tract, the corpus callosum's largest single commissure alongside forceps minor (connecting the frontal lobes, via the genu).
concepts.explicit_objective: State that forceps major is a commissural fibre of the corpus callosum connecting the two occipital lobes.
concepts.pitfalls: Confusing forceps major (splenium fibres to the occipital lobes) with forceps minor (genu fibres to the frontal lobes) — both are corpus callosum commissural tracts named by the U-shaped ('forceps') curve of their fibres but connect different lobes.
concepts.original_wording: Source item 22 ("forceps major / Which of the following is a commissural fiber"), embedded-answer format, read from EOM - paper 2 cns 2019.pdf, p3.
concepts.asu_field_note: Tested as item 22 of EOM - paper 2 cns 2019.pdf (src_c0416316a05f729b9aaf), p3.

concepts.label: Isoflurane is contraindicated (used with caution) in patients with ischaemic heart disease because of coronary steal
concepts.article_title: Isoflurane and coronary steal in ischaemic heart disease
concepts.definition: Isoflurane is a volatile (inhalational) general anaesthetic. Its most clinically important cardiovascular property is coronary vasodilation, which in patients with existing coronary artery disease can produce "coronary steal": blood is diverted away from already-narrowed, poorly-autoregulating stenotic vessels toward normal vessels that dilate more readily, worsening perfusion to the ischaemic myocardial territory. For this reason isoflurane is used with particular caution, or avoided, in patients with significant ischaemic heart disease, in favour of anaesthetics with a more neutral coronary vascular profile.
concepts.explicit_objective: State that isoflurane is contraindicated (used with caution) in patients with ischaemic heart disease because of coronary steal.
concepts.pitfalls: Attributing isoflurane's cardiac risk in ischaemic heart disease to direct myocardial depression rather than to coronary steal (vasodilation redistributing flow away from stenotic, poorly-autoregulating vessels), which is the specific, testable mechanism.
concepts.original_wording: Source item 25 ("isoflurine / Contraindicated anaesthesia in a person suffering from ISHDs"), embedded-answer format, read from EOM - paper 2 cns 2019.pdf, p3.
concepts.asu_field_note: Tested as item 25 of EOM - paper 2 cns 2019.pdf (src_c0416316a05f729b9aaf), p3.

concepts.label: Long-term haloperidol therapy causes tardive dyskinesia, presenting with orofacial involuntary movements
concepts.definition: Haloperidol is a typical (first-generation) antipsychotic and potent dopamine D2 receptor antagonist. Long-term (chronic) use causes tardive dyskinesia, a movement disorder characterised by involuntary, repetitive orofacial movements (lip smacking, tongue protrusion, chewing) and sometimes limb/trunk choreoathetoid movements, attributed to dopamine receptor up-regulation/supersensitivity in the striatum after prolonged blockade. Tardive dyskinesia is often irreversible even after stopping the drug, distinguishing it from haloperidol's earlier, reversible extrapyramidal side effects (acute dystonia, parkinsonism, akathisia).
concepts.explicit_objective: State that long-term haloperidol therapy causes tardive dyskinesia, presenting with orofacial involuntary movements.
concepts.pitfalls: Confusing tardive dyskinesia (a late, often-irreversible complication of chronic antipsychotic use, orofacial choreoathetoid movements) with the earlier, reversible extrapyramidal effects of antipsychotics (acute dystonia, parkinsonism, akathisia), which occur within days to weeks rather than after long-term therapy.
concepts.original_wording: Source item 26 ("halopridol / Longterm antipsychotics then suffered from orofacial involuntary movements typical extrapyramidal effects the drug is"), embedded-answer format, read from EOM - paper 2 cns 2019.pdf, p3.
concepts.asu_field_note: Tested as item 26 of EOM - paper 2 cns 2019.pdf (src_c0416316a05f729b9aaf), p3.

concepts.label: Natalizumab, a monthly intravenous infusion, is used for multiple sclerosis when first-line therapy fails
concepts.article_title: Natalizumab as second-line therapy for multiple sclerosis
concepts.definition: Natalizumab is a monoclonal antibody against alpha-4 integrin, blocking leukocyte adhesion and migration across the blood-brain barrier and so reducing new inflammatory demyelinating activity in multiple sclerosis. It is reserved as a second-line, highly-effective disease-modifying therapy, used when a patient has an inadequate response to (fails) first-line agents, and is given as a monthly intravenous infusion; its use is limited by the risk of progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML), a serious JC virus-related brain infection, which requires monitoring.
concepts.explicit_objective: State that natalizumab is used for multiple sclerosis, given as a monthly intravenous infusion, when first-line therapy fails.
concepts.pitfalls: Confusing natalizumab (a second-line, monthly-infusion disease-modifying therapy for ongoing MS management) with high-dose IV methylprednisolone (used for acute MS relapses/attacks, a different treatment for a different purpose in the same disease).
concepts.original_wording: Source item 28 ("natalizumab / Failure of first line of ttt in multiple sclerosis IV infusion monthly"), embedded-answer format, read from EOM - paper 2 cns 2019.pdf, p3.
concepts.asu_field_note: Tested as item 28 of EOM - paper 2 cns 2019.pdf (src_c0416316a05f729b9aaf), p3.

concepts.label: Ethosuximide is the safest antiepileptic drug for absence epilepsy in a child, with the least effect on cognition and learning
concepts.article_title: Ethosuximide as the safest agent for childhood absence epilepsy
concepts.definition: Ethosuximide blocks T-type calcium channels in thalamic neurons, the specific mechanism underlying the thalamocortical oscillations of absence (petit mal) seizures, and is a first-line drug for absence epilepsy uncomplicated by other seizure types. In children, it is regarded as the safest of the available options for absence epilepsy, with a more favourable cognitive/learning side-effect profile than alternatives such as valproate (which carries broader systemic and teratogenic risk) or older agents, making it the preferred choice when sparing a child's cognition and learning is a priority.
concepts.explicit_objective: State that ethosuximide is the safest antiepileptic for absence epilepsy in a child, with the least effect on cognition and learning.
concepts.pitfalls: Confusing ethosuximide's narrow, T-type-calcium-channel-specific use in absence epilepsy with broader-spectrum antiepileptics such as valproate, which also cover absence seizures but carry a less favourable cognitive and, in females, teratogenic/reproductive safety profile.
concepts.original_wording: Source item 30 ("EthoSuxamide / Safest drug in a child with abSEncE epilepsy with least effects on cognitive and learning functions"), embedded-answer format, read from EOM - paper 2 cns 2019.pdf, p3-4.
concepts.asu_field_note: Tested as item 30 of EOM - paper 2 cns 2019.pdf (src_c0416316a05f729b9aaf), p3-4.

concepts.label: Growth hormone secretion decreases during REM sleep, peaking instead during slow-wave (deep, non-REM) sleep
concepts.article_title: Growth hormone secretion across the sleep cycle
concepts.definition: Growth hormone secretion follows a pulsatile pattern strongly linked to the sleep cycle: the largest, most reliable pulse of growth hormone release occurs during slow-wave (deep, non-REM, stage N3) sleep, early in the night. Correspondingly, growth hormone secretion decreases during REM sleep, when the EEG desynchronises and many other neuroendocrine/autonomic patterns shift markedly from the deep non-REM state. This sleep-stage-linked secretion pattern is one reason adequate slow-wave sleep is considered important for normal growth hormone-dependent processes such as childhood growth and tissue repair.
concepts.explicit_objective: State that growth hormone secretion decreases during REM sleep and peaks during slow-wave (deep) sleep.
concepts.pitfalls: Confusing growth hormone's sleep-stage pattern (peaks in slow-wave/deep non-REM sleep, decreases in REM) with other hormones/processes that instead peak during or are characteristic of REM sleep, or with sleepwalking, a distinct slow-wave-sleep parasomnia unrelated to hormone secretion.
concepts.original_wording: Source item 32 ("growth hormone / Dec in REM sleep"), embedded-answer format, read from EOM - paper 2 cns 2019.pdf, p4.
concepts.asu_field_note: Tested as item 32 of EOM - paper 2 cns 2019.pdf (src_c0416316a05f729b9aaf), p4.

concepts.label: The anterior hypothalamus is the heat-loss (cooling) centre responsible for thermoregulation, not for generating fever in response to infection or inflammation
concepts.article_title: The anterior hypothalamus and heat-loss thermoregulation
concepts.definition: The hypothalamus is the body's principal thermoregulatory centre, with anterior and posterior regions playing complementary roles: the anterior hypothalamus (anterior/preoptic area) functions as the heat-loss centre, triggering cooling responses (cutaneous vasodilation, sweating) when core temperature rises, while the posterior hypothalamus functions as the heat-conservation/heat-generation centre. Because the anterior hypothalamus is not itself an infection/inflammation sensor, a rise in temperature that follows direct anterior hypothalamic injury (for example after trauma, as in a fall from a bicycle) reflects a thermoregulatory set-point/heat-loss failure rather than a true infective or inflammatory fever, an important clinical distinction.
concepts.explicit_objective: State that the anterior hypothalamus functions as the heat-loss centre for thermoregulation.
concepts.pitfalls: Confusing the anterior hypothalamus (heat-loss/cooling centre) with the posterior hypothalamus (heat-conservation/generation centre) — the two subregions have opposite thermoregulatory roles, and a lesion of one produces the deficit expected of losing the other's opposing function.
concepts.original_wording: Source item 34 ("anterior hypothalamus / [fall from bicycle, fever without infection or inflammation because this centre was struck and its temperature raised]"), embedded-answer format, read from EOM - paper 2 cns 2019.pdf, p4.
concepts.asu_field_note: Tested as item 34 of EOM - paper 2 cns 2019.pdf (src_c0416316a05f729b9aaf), p4.

concepts.label: Delta waves on the EEG characterise deep (slow-wave, stage N3) sleep
concepts.article_title: Delta waves as the EEG signature of deep sleep
concepts.definition: EEG rhythms are classified by frequency and amplitude, and each is characteristic of a particular state of arousal. Delta waves are the lowest-frequency (under 4 Hz), highest-amplitude EEG rhythm, and they characterise deep, slow-wave sleep (stage N3 of non-REM sleep) — the stage with the highest arousal threshold, in which someone is hardest to wake. This contrasts with the faster, lower-amplitude, desynchronised EEG pattern of REM sleep, which paradoxically resembles the waking EEG despite REM being a deep sleep stage behaviourally.
concepts.explicit_objective: State that delta waves on the EEG characterise deep (slow-wave) sleep.
concepts.pitfalls: Confusing delta waves (lowest frequency, deep slow-wave sleep, highest arousal threshold) with the fast, desynchronised, wake-like EEG pattern of REM sleep — the two are near-opposite EEG signatures despite both occurring during sleep.
concepts.original_wording: Source item 35 ("DElta wave / Deep sleep"), embedded-answer format, read from EOM - paper 2 cns 2019.pdf, p4.
concepts.asu_field_note: Tested as item 35 of EOM - paper 2 cns 2019.pdf (src_c0416316a05f729b9aaf), p4.

concepts.label: Explicit (declarative) memory is exemplified by the conscious recall of a personal event, such as remembering a birthday
concepts.article_title: Explicit memory as conscious recall of personal events
concepts.definition: Long-term memory is broadly divided into explicit (declarative) memory, which can be consciously recalled and verbally described, and implicit (non-declarative) memory, which is expressed through performance (skills, habits, conditioning) without conscious recall. Explicit memory further divides into episodic memory (personal experiences/events, tied to a specific time and place) and semantic memory (general facts and knowledge). Consciously recalling a specific personal event, such as remembering one's own tenth birthday, is a classic example of episodic explicit memory: it requires deliberate, conscious retrieval and is anatomically dependent on the medial temporal lobe/hippocampal system.
concepts.explicit_objective: State that explicit (declarative) memory is exemplified by the conscious recall of a personal event.
concepts.pitfalls: Confusing explicit/episodic memory (conscious recall of a specific personal event) with semantic memory (general facts/knowledge, also explicit but not tied to a specific personal experience) or with implicit memory (skills/habits, expressed through performance without conscious recall).
concepts.original_wording: Source item 36 ("teenager remembers her 10th birthday / Explicit memory conscious recall example"), embedded-answer format, read from EOM - paper 2 cns 2019.pdf, p4.
concepts.asu_field_note: Tested as item 36 of EOM - paper 2 cns 2019.pdf (src_c0416316a05f729b9aaf), p4.

concepts.label: Consolidation of memory (converting short-term into stable long-term memory) is a function of the limbic system
concepts.article_title: Memory consolidation as a limbic system function
concepts.definition: Memory consolidation is the process by which a newly formed, initially fragile short-term memory trace is stabilised into a durable long-term memory. This process depends on the limbic system, chiefly the hippocampus and adjacent medial temporal lobe structures (parahippocampal, entorhinal cortex) together with the fornix and mammillary bodies of the Papez circuit, which bind together the distributed cortical representations of an experience into a lasting memory over time (a process aided by sleep). Damage to these limbic structures, as in bilateral hippocampal lesions, characteristically impairs the ability to consolidate new memories (anterograde amnesia) while often sparing older, already-consolidated memories.
concepts.explicit_objective: State that consolidation of memory is a function of the limbic system.
concepts.pitfalls: Confusing memory consolidation (a limbic/hippocampal function, converting short-term to long-term memory) with the storage of already-consolidated long-term memories, which is thought to be distributed across the neocortex rather than remaining dependent on the hippocampus indefinitely.
concepts.original_wording: Source item 38 ("consolidation of memory / Function of Limbic System"), embedded-answer format, read from EOM - paper 2 cns 2019.pdf, p4.
concepts.asu_field_note: Tested as item 38 of EOM - paper 2 cns 2019.pdf (src_c0416316a05f729b9aaf), p4.
